title: The TMS-evoked potential: recovering the canonical TEP component sequence from real TMS-EEG

dataset.name: TESA example TMS-EEG data (Rogasch et al.)
dataset.record: one healthy participant, 150 single TMS pulses over left superior parietal cortex (MNI -20/-65/65) at 0.2 Hz; 59-channel EEG, 1000 Hz, epoched -250..450 ms around the pulse
dataset.citation: Rogasch NC, Sullivan C, Thomson RH, et al. Analysing concurrent transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroencephalographic data: A review and introduction to the open-source TESA software. NeuroImage 2017;147:934-951. Example data: figshare doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.3188800 (GPL 2.0+).

proposition: A single TMS pulse over the cortex sets off a stereotyped chain of EEG deflections -- the TMS-evoked potential (TEP) -- whose components (N15, P30, N45, P60, N100, P180) are the canonical read-out of cortical reactivity. Running the ecosystem's TEP pipeline on the real TESA TMS-EEG recording (150 pulses, 59 channels), all six components are recovered in their correct CANONICAL TEMPORAL ORDER -- median latencies 16 < 31 < 45 < 66 < 115 < 188 ms, monotonically increasing -- and with their correct POLARITIES: across channels, the peak in each window carries its expected sign (negative for N-, positive for P-) in 88-97% of channels (mean 92%). The late N100 (~115 ms) and P180 (~188 ms) sit exactly where the literature places them. The component windows say WHERE to look; the polarities and the peaks are the data's own.

claims.statement: median latency of the N100 component (the hallmark late TEP peak), ms
median latency of the P180 component, ms
the six components appear in canonical temporal order (latencies monotonically increasing; 1=yes)
mean across-channel polarity-match rate (%): the peak sign matches the expected N/P

validation.reference: The TMS-evoked potential is an established, stereotyped response: a canonical sequence of components (N15, P30, N45, P60, N100, P180) at characteristic latencies and alternating polarities, the P60/N100/P180 being the robust late peaks (Rogasch, Ilmoniemi). A correct implementation must recover (1) all six components, (2) in the correct temporal ORDER, and (3) with the correct POLARITIES -- which the ecosystem does: median latencies 16/31/45/66/115/188 ms (monotonic), and 88-97% of channels carry the expected sign per component (mean 92%); the N100 (~115 ms) and P180 (~188 ms) match the literature.
validation.data: REAL -- TESA example TMS-EEG (Rogasch et al., figshare 3188800), one participant, 150 TMS pulses, 59-channel EEG
validation.note: The reproducible finding is the canonical TEP component sequence -- six components in the right temporal ORDER with the right POLARITIES (mean 92% across-channel match), the N100/P180 at their literature latencies. HONEST scope: (1) SINGLE participant/session; (2) stimulation was over left PARIETAL cortex (the TESA example), not motor cortex -- the TEP is a general cortical-reactivity read-out; (3) the source data is the TESA 'cut/interpolated/downsampled' file (the large early pulse artifact was already removed at source), so this case validates the COMPONENT-EXTRACTION step, not TMS-artifact removal (PhysioNeurophys provides removeTMSpulse()/tmsSSPSIR() for that); (4) the component WINDOWS are fixed a priori (so a component's latency lies within its window by construction) -- the non-trivial, data-driven results are the correct POLARITIES and the monotonic ordering across the six windows; (5) baseline -200..-20 ms.

open_questions.q: Motor-cortex stimulation with concurrent EMG (the MEP + the TEP together), the full TMS-artifact-removal pipeline (removeTMSpulse -> tmsSSPSIR -> ICA) from the raw recording, and a group-level TEP would extend this to a complete TMS-EEG workflow. Documented, not escalated.
